passage: At home in the flat, Naveen, five, held up a spoon of peas. "If I eat peas, can I have a sticker?" His father Suraj smiled. "Peas first. Stickers are for the chart on Sundays." "Just one sticker. Please. One." "Not tonight. But if you eat a few peas, you can pick the bedtime story." Naveen counted five peas into his mouth. "Story!"

qa.q: What did Naveen want in return for eating peas?
qa.a: A sticker.

qa.q: What might Naveen be feeling as he offers the trade, and what does he want?
qa.a: He is probably hopeful and eager to get a sticker for eating peas he dislikes. He may also have been testing whether the trade would work.

qa.q: How did Suraj hold the limit kindly?
qa.a: He said no to the sticker but offered a different reward, picking the bedtime story.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel about the trade?
qa.a: Probably amused and patient, since he smiled and offered another option.

grounding: Shows a preschooler pleading and offering a simple bargain, with a parent holding the limit kindly and rewarding flexibility.

passage:
"Please, one more turn!" said Nitin, five, on the park slide.
"The timer's done. Time to go," said his mother Hafsa.
"I'll give you my biscuit if I get one more turn."
Hafsa laughed. "A biscuit for a turn? That's a clever trade, but it's time to go home."
"Then tomorrow I go first?"
"Tomorrow you can have the first turn, if we come at our usual time."
"Deal!"

qa.q: What did Nitin offer Hafsa?
qa.a: His biscuit.

qa.q: What does Nitin's offer of the biscuit suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: That he is trying a trade to get what he wants, showing a growing sense of exchange. He might also have been worried about the fun ending.

qa.q: How did Hafsa keep the limit and still reward flexibility?
qa.a: She said it was time to go now but agreed to a first turn tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel about Nitin's trade?
qa.a: Amused, since she laughed, though she stayed firm.

grounding: Shows a preschooler pleading and bargaining for one more turn, with a parent holding the limit and offering a fair alternative.

passage:
Note by Anand, preschool teacher.
At tidy-up time, Wasim said, “Please, one more minute on the swing!” I said no, it was time. Then he tried: “If I tidy all the blocks, can I have the first swing tomorrow?” I thought it was a fair deal, and a sign he's learning to trade. I said, “Yes, if you tidy the blocks.” He did, very fast, and reminded me three times before home time. Tomorrow I'll keep my word, so he learns bargains are real.

qa.q: What did Wasim offer to tidy?
qa.a: All the blocks.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he offered the deal?
qa.a: He was hopeful and eager, still wanting the swing and trying a new way to get it after pleading didn't work.

qa.q: Why does Anand plan to keep the promise tomorrow?
qa.a: So Wasim learns that fair bargains are real and trustworthy, which rewards his flexibility sensibly.

qa.q: How might other children see Wasim's deal?
qa.a: They might see it as a clever idea and try making fair deals too.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler move from pleading to simple bargaining, and a kind limit plus a fair reward.

passage: At the weekly fair in the small town, Nikita rode the little merry-go-round twice. “Please, Amma, one more! Just one!” Irawati shook her head. “Two was the plan. No more today.” Nikita tried again. “I'll carry the vegetable bag all the way home if I get one more.” Irawati smiled at the idea but held firm. “No more rides today. But I like your offer. You can carry the bag, and you choose the sweet at the shop.” Nikita thought, then grabbed the bag. “Jalebi!”

qa.q: How many times had Nikita ridden the merry-go-round?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she offered to carry the bag?
qa.a: She was hopeful and eager for another ride, trying a trade after her pleading didn't work.

qa.q: How did Irawati hold the limit kindly while rewarding flexibility?
qa.a: She kept the no on rides but praised the offer and let Nikita choose the sweet for carrying the bag.

qa.q: What would change if Irawati had given in to the pleading?
qa.a: Nikita would learn that pleading enough changes a no, making the next outing harder.

grounding: A preschooler pleads and then bargains for another ride, and her mother holds the limit kindly while rewarding flexibility.

passage: At dinner in Buenos Aires, Santiago pushed his peas around. “Please, Papa, no peas. Please!” Yosef said, “Five peas.” Santiago thought. “If I eat five peas, can I get a sticker?” Yosef laughed. “Deal. Five peas, one sticker.” Santiago counted out loud and ate them with dramatic faces. He got his sticker, a green frog. Then he asked, “If I eat ten, can I get two?” Yosef shook his head, smiling. “Five was the deal for tonight.”

qa.q: What was on Santiago's sticker?
qa.a: A green frog.

qa.q: What was Santiago feeling when he asked for two stickers for ten peas?
qa.a: He felt pleased and bold after his first deal worked, and was testing whether he could get more.

qa.q: How did Yosef balance the bargain and the limit?
qa.a: He accepted a fair first deal and gave the sticker, but kept the limit when Santiago tried to push for more.

qa.q: How might Yosef see Santiago's bargaining?
qa.a: He finds it funny and a sign Santiago is learning to trade, which is why he smiled.

grounding: A preschooler pleads and then bargains peas for a sticker, and his father rewards flexibility sensibly but holds a limit.

passage:
Story time at the community library was over. Sudha Aunty closed the book.

"Please, one more! Just one more, please!" Urmila begged, hands clasped.

"Not today. Story time has finished."

Urmila thought hard. "If I put all the cushions back, can we have one more?"

Sudha Aunty smiled. "That's a clever offer. The answer is still no more stories today. But if you help with the cushions, you can choose the first book for next week."

Urmila weighed it up. Then she grabbed the biggest cushion. "Deal!"

She stacked every cushion, and chose the dinosaur book for the next week.

qa.q: Which book did Urmila choose for the next week?
qa.a: The dinosaur book.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she offered to put the cushions back?
qa.a: She was most likely eager for more stories and hopeful that a trade might change the answer. Grabbing the biggest cushion shows she felt pleased with the new deal.

qa.q: How did Sudha Aunty hold the limit kindly while rewarding flexibility?
qa.a: She praised the clever offer but kept "no more stories today", then offered a sensible reward, choosing next week's first book, for helping.

qa.q: What would change if Sudha Aunty had read one more because Urmila bargained?
qa.a: Urmila might learn that bargaining always changes a no, and try it every time story time ends.

grounding: It shows a preschooler pleading for one more story and offering a simple trade, and an adult holding the limit kindly while rewarding her flexibility sensibly.
